Executive Summary
Purpose
●
Gen Z is shifting to a more 
active and 
health-conscious lifestyle
●
Spending too much on 
supplements
●
Cheap and convenient 
solution to supplements
Key Findings
●
Price is the most important 
attribute
○
Very price sensitive
●
Two Segments
○
Price-Conscious
○
Customizers

Background and Business Context
Since the pandemic, health and 
wellness has become increasingly 
more popular in the U.S.. 
Consumers have taken their health 
more seriously, and are looking for 
“preventative” healthcare, instead 
of reactive.
This increase in health conscious 
consumers has sparked major 
growth in the dietary supplement 
market. 
Current Market (2025) 
USD 145.62 Billion
Projected Market (2030) 
USD 179.36 Billion
Growth Rate (2025-2030)
4.62% CAGR
(Mordor Intelligence)

Background and Business Context
The dietary supplement market is 
currently dominated by Amway 
Corporation, Herbalife, and 
Nestlé. 
These companies have started to 
integrate gummy supplements into 
their product segments, but the 
customization of these gummy 
supplements remains limited.
According to Grand View 
Research, younger generations in 
particular are more likely to prefer 
supplements that are personalized 
and in gummy form.
Thus, we decided to distinguish 
Gummy Gains from its 
competitors by giving consumers 
customized gummy supplements.

Methodology and Overview
To understand consumer 
preferences for gummy 
supplements, we conducted a 
choice-based conjoint analysis. 
With this survey we hoped to 
answer:
“What do Gen-Z 
consumers value most 
when choosing gummy 
supplements?”
Target Market: Gen Z (ages 13-28 
years old) – health conscious 
consumers.
To get responses from our Gen Z 
target market, we sent out our 
survey to the RIT baseball team, 
friends and peers at RIT, and we 
also posted the survey on social 
media. 
In the end we gathered a total of 
35 respondents.

Methodology and Overview
1)
Price  –  low (<$10),  medium 
($10-$25),  high (>$25)
2)
Contents  –  one supplement 
(predetermined),  two 
supplements 
(predetermined), 
customizable supplements 
(can choose two 
supplements)
3) Flavor  –  blue raspberry,  
cherry, orange,  watermelon,  
mixed/assorted
4) Sweetness  –  low sugar (<5g), 
sugar-free (0g),  mild sweetness 
(5-10g),  extra sweet (>10g)
Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis
4 Attributes and 15 Levels

●

●
Customizable two supplements
●
Flavor variety 
●

●
50 supplement containers
Product

Marketing Efforts

Limitations 
●
Limited sample size (n=35)
●
Lack of representativeness 
for Gen Z
●
Sampling bias
○
42.86% of 
respondents play 
varsity sports. 
○
54.29% of 
respondents go to 
RIT.
●
Underestimated the cost of 
creating out product (low 
price point <$10 is not 
realistic)
●
Left out detailed supplement 
contents (e.g. whey protein, 
caffeine, vitamin d, etc.)
●
Allowing respondents to mix 
supplements together could 
pose risk

Considerations
In the future, we should also run A/B 
tests to optimize our sales process to 
see which segment satisﬁes 
consumers the most.
 In addition, we should use an A/B 
test to test our marketing and 
messaging, particularly on social 
media, to better understand what 
resonates with our audience and 
what doesn’t.
We should consider researching the 
effectiveness / cost of mixing 
supplements together and putting 
them into gummy form.
Research on combining creatine and 
protein (recovery), caffeine and 
citrulline (morning), and melatonin 
and magnesium (sleep).
